# Thought experiment (`thought_experiment`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/ideas.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Scientific method & philosophical ideas (`ideas`)
- Deps: helped by formal_logic
- Core idea: Imagine a precisely specified situation and reason out what must happen in order to expose a contradiction in a theory or to isolate what matters. Galileo's case against 'heavier falls faster': tie a light stone to a heavy one; the slow one should hold the fast one back, yet the pair is heavier and should fall faster, so the premise defeats itself. Another is his ship: below deck on a smoothly moving ship, drops still fall straight and flies fly alike in all directions, so steady motion cannot be felt and the earth may move. Such arguments cost nothing and work in any language, but they only show what follows from assumptions and should be followed by a real test.
- Pitfalls:
  - Treating a thought experiment as proof about the world; in air a heavy ball does land slightly before a light one
  - Telling the Leaning Tower of Pisa drop as fact; it rests on a late account by Viviani, while Stevin and de Groot really dropped lead balls at Delft in 1586
  - Smuggling modern intuitions (frictionless planes, empty space) into the set-up as if they were obvious to the listener
  - Mocking Aristotle: his rule describes bodies sinking through a resisting medium reasonably well
- History: greece: c. 450 BC – Zeno's paradoxes; c. 400 BC Archytas asks what happens when one stretches a hand beyond the edge of the universe; china: c. 300 BC – paradoxes of Hui Shi and Gongsun Long; Zhuangzi's butterfly dream; india: c. 100 BC–200 AD – the chariot argument about the self in the Questions of King Milinda; egypt: c. 530 AD – John Philoponus of Alexandria argues from actual drops that unequal weights fall almost together; islamic: c. 1020 – Ibn Sina's 'floating man' argument for self-awareness; europe: c. 1350–1377 – Buridan and Oresme argue about a rotating earth with arrows and ships; 1586 Stevin's chain on a prism; 1632–1638 Galileo; 1867 Maxwell's demon; 1897 Mach popularises the term 'Gedankenexperiment'
- Read:
  - Galileo Galilei, Dialogo sopra i due massimi sistemi del mondo (1632)
  - James Robert Brown, The Laboratory of the Mind: Thought Experiments in the Natural Sciences (1991)
